newsitem.title: ITALY: Exiled Cubans, awaiting Castro, protest to Pope.
newsitem.headline: Exiled Cubans, awaiting Castro, protest to Pope.

text.p: About 80 Cuban exiles denouncing alleged human rights abuses took their "pilgrimage of pain" to Pope John Paul on Wednesday ahead of the expected arrival of communist leader Fidel Castro in Rome for a World Food Summit.

The group, most of whom live in Miami, included a man who lost his wife and 11-year-old son as they were trying to flee to the United States in a boat and a former comrade-in-arms of Castro who was later jailed for 30 years.
They attended the Pontiff's weekly general audience at the Vatican and one of them, Dalia Santana, 81 and wheelchair-bound, was greeted by the Pope.

"I pray for Cuba every day," he told her as she displayed a sheet signed in jail by 82 political prisoners and decorated with a picture of the Madonna and the words "Para Amor, Libertad, Democracia" (For Love, Liberty, Democracy).

Castro on Wednesday was given a prominent role at the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit, which opened with an address from the Pope, when he was named one of the six vice-chairmen for the five-day gathering.
Food Industry Minister Alejandro Roca Iglesias, not Castro, was officially listed as head of the Cuban delegation.
Castro's movements are always cloaked in strict secrecy. However, diplomatic sources said the 70-year-old communist was expected to arrive in Rome early on Friday.
All eyes will be on whether Castro, an atheist whose government has a difficult relationship with the Roman Catholic Church despite recent signs of openness, has an audience with the Pope.

"Castro wants to make it a meeting between the grand old man of socialism and the grand old man of the Church," said Miguel Angel Loredo, a Franciscan monk who served 10 years hard labour in Cuba from 1966-76 on what he called "fabricated" charges.
"He wants the big picture -- the fighter for people in the world, a Mother Theresa of Calcutta with a beard...and the Pope," Loredo told Reuters. "Castro is a great dealer."
The Pope is expected to meet Castro later this week, opening the way for his first visit to the Caribbean island.

Sergio Perodin broke down and wept uncontrollably for several minutes as he told a news conference how, in July 1994, the small tug on which he was trying to flee sank after boats pursuing it targetted it with powerful jets of water.
"All you could hear were mothers shouting out for their children," he said. Less than half those aboard survived.
"The thing that hurts me most is that the world keeps silent about the crimes that the government of Cuba commits," he said.
Mario Chanas de Armas, who met Castro in 1952 and took part in his first attempts to overthrow dictator Fulgencio Batista four years later, said Cuba had been "betrayed by Castro".
Chanas de Armas was arrested in 1961, two years after Castro finally won power, and served 30 years in jail on charges of allegedly taking part in an assassination plot.
Castro will be buoyed in Rome by an overwhelming vote on Tuesday in the U.N. General Assembly in favour of ending a 34-year U.S. trade embargo to try to force him out of power.
But Castro came under pressure from leaders of other Latin American countries, Spain and Portugal at a summit in Chile this week urged reform to the political system he has led for 37 years.
